title: Chapter 22. Of Systems Subject, Political, and Private
paragraphs: Having spoken of the generation, form, and power of a commonwealth, I am next in order to speak of its parts. And first of systems, which resemble the similar parts, or the muscles, of a natural body. By SYSTEMS I understand any number of men joined in one interest, or in one piece of business. Of these, some are regular and some irregular. Regular are those in which one man, or one assembly of men, is constituted as the representative of the whole number. All others are irregular.

Of regular systems, some are absolute and independent, subject to no one but their own representative — and such are only commonwealths, which I have already spoken of in the five preceding chapters. Others are dependent — that is, subordinate to some sovereign power, to which every one, and also their representative, is subject.

Of subordinate systems, some are political and some private. Political systems (otherwise called bodies politic, or persons in law) are those made by authority from the sovereign power of the commonwealth. Private systems are those constituted by subjects among themselves, or by authority from a foreigner. For no authority derived from a foreign power is, within the dominion of another, public there; it is private.

And of private systems, some are lawful and some unlawful. Lawful are those allowed by the commonwealth; all others are unlawful. Irregular systems are those which, having no representative, consist only in the gathering of people. These, if not forbidden by the commonwealth and not formed for any evil purpose (such as crowds gathering at markets, or shows, or for any other harmless end), are lawful. But when the intention is evil, or (if the number is significant) unknown, they are unlawful.

In bodies politic, the power of the representative is always limited; and what prescribes its limits is the sovereign power. For unlimited power is absolute sovereignty. And the sovereign, in every commonwealth, is the absolute representative of all the subjects; so no other person can be the representative of any part of them except so far as the sovereign gives leave. To give a body politic of subjects leave to have an absolute representative for all intents and purposes would be to abandon that much of the government of the commonwealth, and to divide the dominion, contrary to the subjects' peace and defence — which cannot be understood as the sovereign's intention in any grant that does not plainly and directly discharge them from their subjection. For the inferred consequences of words are not signs of his will when other consequences are signs of the contrary; they are rather signs of error and miscalculation, to which all mankind is too prone.

The bounds of that power which is given to the representative of a body politic are to be noticed from two sources. One is the writ, or letters, from the sovereign; the other is the law of the commonwealth.

For though in the institution or acquisition of a commonwealth, which is independent, there is no need of any written document — because the power of the representative there has no other bounds than those set by the unwritten law of nature — yet in subordinate bodies there are such various limitations necessary about their business, times, and places that they can neither be remembered without letters, nor heeded unless those letters are public — letters patent, that they may be read out to them, and sealed or otherwise marked with the seals or other permanent signs of the sovereign authority.

And because such limitation is not always easy, or perhaps possible, to be set down in writing, the ordinary laws common to all subjects must determine what the representative may lawfully do in all cases where the letters themselves are silent. And therefore —
When the representative is one man, his unauthorised acts are his alone.

In a body politic, if the representative is one man, whatever he does in the person of the body that is not warranted in his letters, nor by the laws, is his own act, and not the act of the body, nor of any other member besides himself. For beyond the limits set by his letters, or by the laws, he represents no man's person but his own. But what he does in keeping with them is the act of every one. For of the sovereign's act every one is the author, because the sovereign is their unlimited representative; and the act of one who does not depart from the sovereign's letters is the sovereign's act, and so every member of the body is the author of it.
When the representative is an assembly, the act binds only those who assented.

But if the representative is an assembly, then whatever that assembly shall decree, when not warranted by their letters or by the laws, is the act of the assembly, or body politic, and the act of every one by whose vote the decree was made — but not the act of any man who, being present, voted against it, nor of any man who was absent, unless he voted by proxy. It is the act of the assembly because it was voted by the majority; and if it is a crime, the assembly may be punished, so far as it is capable — by dissolution, or by forfeiture of their letters (which to such artificial and fictitious bodies amounts to a capital sentence), or (if the assembly has a common stock in which none of the innocent members has property) by a fine. For from corporal penalties nature has exempted all bodies politic. But those who did not give their vote are innocent, because the assembly cannot represent any man in matters unwarranted by their letters, and so the dissenters and absentees are not implicated in their votes.

When the representative is one man, and he borrows money or comes into debt by contract, he alone is liable; the members are not. If the person of a body politic, being in one man, borrows money from a stranger — that is, from one who is not of the same body (no letters need limit borrowing, since it is left to the lender's own inclinations to limit lending) — the debt is the representative's. For if he had authority from his letters to make the members pay what he borrowed, he would in consequence have sovereignty over them; and so the grant would either be void as proceeding from error (a thing commonly incident to human nature), as not being a sufficient sign of the will of the grantor, or, if it were avowed by him, then the representative would be sovereign, and would not fall under the present question (which is only about subordinate bodies). No member is therefore obliged to pay the debt so borrowed; only the representative is. Because the one who lent it, being a stranger to the letters and to the qualifications of the body, takes for his debtors only those who are engaged; and since the representative can engage himself and no one else, the lender has only him for debtor — who must therefore pay him, out of the common stock if there is any, or, if there is none, out of his own estate.
If the representative comes into debt by contract, or by being fined, the case is the same.
When the representative is an assembly, only those who assented are liable.

When the representative is an assembly, and the debt is to a stranger, all those, and only those, are responsible for the debt who gave their votes either to the borrowing of it, or to the contract that made it due, or to the act for which the fine was imposed. For every one of those, by voting, engaged himself for the payment. For he who is the author of the borrowing is obliged to the payment of the whole debt, even though, when paid by any one, the rest are discharged.
If the debt is to one of the assembly, only the body is obliged.

But if the debt is to one of the assembly, the assembly alone is obliged to the payment out of their common stock (if they have any). For having the liberty to vote, if he votes that the money shall be borrowed, he votes that it shall be paid; and if he votes that it shall not be borrowed, or is absent, yet because in lending he votes for the borrowing, he contradicts his earlier vote, and is obliged by the later one, and becomes both borrower and lender. Consequently he cannot demand payment from any particular man, but only from the common treasury; and if that fails, he has no remedy and no complaint, except against himself. Being privy to the assembly's acts and to their means of payment, and not being compelled, he nevertheless, through his own folly, lent his money.

Sometimes lawful; but against sovereign power never. It is plain from this that in bodies politic subordinate, subject to a sovereign power, it is sometimes not only lawful but expedient for a particular man to make open protest against the decrees of the representative assembly, and to have his dissent recorded, or to call witnesses to it; otherwise he may be obliged to pay debts contracted, or be held responsible for crimes committed, by other men. But in a sovereign assembly that liberty is taken away — both because anyone who protests there denies their sovereignty, and because whatever is commanded by the sovereign power is, as far as the subject is concerned (though not always so in the sight of God), justified by the command, since of such command every subject is the author.

The variety of bodies politic is almost infinite. They are distinguished not only by the various affairs for which they are constituted — in which there is an unspeakable diversity — but also by the times, places, and numbers, all subject to many limitations. As to their affairs, some are ordained for government. For instance, the government of a province may be committed to an assembly of men in which all resolutions are to depend on the votes of the majority; and then that assembly is a body politic, and their power is limited by commission. The word 'province' means a charge, or a care of business, which the one whose business it is commits to another man, to be administered for him and under him. So when in one commonwealth there are various countries that have laws distinct from one another, or are far distant in place, and the administration of government is committed to various persons, those countries where the sovereign is not resident, but governs by commission, are called provinces. But of the government of a province by an assembly residing in the province itself there are few examples. The Romans, who had sovereignty over many provinces, governed them always by presidents and praetors, and not by assemblies, as they governed the city of Rome and the territories adjoining. In the same way, when colonies were sent out from England to plant Virginia and the Somers Islands, though the government of them here was committed to assemblies in London, those assemblies never committed the government under them to any assembly in the colony itself, but sent one governor to each plantation. For though every man, where he can be present by nature, wants to share in the government, yet where they cannot be present, men are also inclined by nature to commit the government of their common interest rather to a monarchical than to a popular form of government. This is also evident in those who have great private estates, who, when unwilling to take the trouble of administering the business that belongs to them, choose rather to trust one servant than an assembly of either friends or servants. But however that may be in fact, we may suppose the government of a province, or colony, to be committed to an assembly; and when it is, what I have to say in this place is this: that whatever debt is contracted by that assembly, or whatever unlawful act is decreed, is the act only of those who assented, and not of any who dissented, or were absent, for the reasons already given. Also, that an assembly residing outside the bounds of the colony it governs cannot exercise any power over the persons or goods of any of the colonists, to seize them for debt or other duty, in any place outside the colony itself, as having no jurisdiction or authority elsewhere; the assembly is left to the remedy which the law of the place allows. And though the assembly has the right to impose a fine on any of its members who shall break the laws they make, yet outside the colony itself they have no right to execute the same. And what is said here about the rights of an assembly for the government of a province or a colony applies also to an assembly for the government of a town, or a university, or a college, or a church, or for any other government over the persons of men.

And in general, in all bodies politic, if any particular member considers himself injured by the body itself, the hearing of his case belongs to the sovereign, and to those whom the sovereign has ordained as judges in such cases, or shall ordain for that particular cause — and not to the body itself. For the whole body in this case is his fellow subject. In a sovereign assembly it is otherwise: for there, if the sovereign is not judge (even in his own cause), there can be no judge at all.

In a body politic for the orderly conduct of foreign trade, the most convenient representative is an assembly of all the members — that is, one at which every man who ventures his money may, if he chooses, be present at all the deliberations and resolutions of the body. To prove this, we should consider the end for which men who are merchants — and who can buy and sell, export and import their merchandise according to their own discretion — nevertheless bind themselves up in one corporation. There are indeed few merchants who, with the merchandise they buy at home, can freight a ship to export it, or with that they buy abroad can freight one to bring it home; and so they have need to join together in one society, where every man may either share in the gain in proportion to his venture, or take his own part and sell what he transports or imports at such prices as he thinks fit. But this is no body politic, since there is no common representative to oblige them to any law other than what is common to all other subjects. The end of their incorporating is to make their gain the greater; and this is done in two ways: by sole buying, and by sole selling, both at home and abroad. So to grant to a company of merchants that they shall be a corporation, or body politic, is to grant them a double monopoly — to be sole buyers, and to be sole sellers. For when there is a company incorporated for any particular foreign country, only its members export the commodities that are saleable in that country; which is sole buying at home and sole selling abroad. At home there is only one buyer, and abroad only one seller: both of which are gainful to the merchant, because by this means they buy at home at lower, and sell abroad at higher, rates. And abroad there is only one buyer of foreign merchandise, and only one seller of it at home: both of which, again, are gainful to the venturers.

Of this double monopoly, one part is disadvantageous to the people at home, the other to foreigners. At home, by their sole right of exporting, they set what price they please on the husbandry and handiwork of the people; and by sole importing, what price they please on all foreign commodities the people need. Both of these are bad for the people. On the other side, by sole selling of native commodities abroad, and sole buying of foreign commodities on the spot, they raise the price of the latter and beat down the price of the former, to the disadvantage of the foreigner: for where there is only one seller, the goods are dearer, and where only one buyer, cheaper. Such corporations therefore are nothing but monopolies — though they would be very profitable for a commonwealth if, being bound up in one body in foreign markets, they were at home left at liberty, every man to buy and sell at whatever price he could.

Since then the end of these bodies of merchants is not a common benefit to the whole body (which in this case has no common stock except what is deducted from each member's particular venture, for building, buying, victualling, and manning ships), but the particular gain of every venturer, it is reasonable that every man should be familiar with the use to which his own money is put — that is, that every one should be part of the assembly that has the power to direct it, and have access to the accounts. So the representative of such a body must be an assembly, at which every member of the body may, if he wishes, be present at the consultations.

If a body politic of merchants contracts a debt to a stranger by the act of their representative assembly, every member is liable individually for the whole. For a stranger can take no notice of their private laws, but regards them as so many particular men, every one obliged to the whole payment, until payment made by one discharges all the rest. But if the debt is to one of the company, the creditor is debtor for the whole to himself, and cannot therefore demand his debt except from the common stock, if there is any.

If the commonwealth lays a tax on the body, it is understood to be laid on every member in proportion to his particular venture in the company. For there is in this case no other common stock than what is made up of their particular ventures.

If a fine is laid on the body for some unlawful act, those alone are liable by whose votes the act was decreed, or by whose assistance it was carried out; for in none of the rest is there any crime except being of the body — and that, if it is a crime (since the body was ordained by the authority of the commonwealth), is not his.

If one of the members is indebted to the body, he may be sued by the body; but his goods cannot be taken, nor his person imprisoned, by the authority of the body — only by the authority of the commonwealth. For if they could do it by their own authority, they could by their own authority give judgement that the debt is due, which is as much as to be judge in their own cause.

These bodies, formed for the government of men or for trade, are either perpetual or for a time prescribed in writing. But there are also bodies whose duration is limited only by the nature of their business. For example, if a sovereign monarch, or a sovereign assembly, thinks fit to command the towns and other parts of his territory to send him their deputies, to inform him of the condition and necessities of the subjects, or to advise with him for the making of good laws, or for any other cause, as with one person representing the whole country, such deputies, having a place and time of meeting assigned to them, are there, and at that time, a body politic, representing every subject of that dominion — but only for such matters as are put to them by the man, or assembly, who by the sovereign authority sent for them. And when it is declared that no more shall be put to them, or debated by them, the body is dissolved. For if they were the absolute representative of the people, they would be the sovereign assembly; and so there would be two sovereign assemblies, or two sovereigns, over the same people — which is incompatible with their peace. And so where there is once a sovereignty, there can be no absolute representation of the people but by it. As for the limits of how far such a body shall represent the whole people, those are set out in the writing by which they were sent for. For the people cannot choose their deputies to any other intent than is expressed in the writing directed to them from their sovereign.

Private bodies that are regular and lawful are those constituted without letters, or any other written authority, beyond the laws common to all other subjects. And because they are united in one person representative, they are held to be regular. Such are all families, in which the father, or master, orders the whole family. For he binds his children and servants, as far as the law permits, though not further — since none of them are bound to obedience in actions the law has forbidden to be done. In all other actions, while they are under domestic government, they are subject to their fathers and masters, as to their immediate sovereigns. For the father and master, being before the institution of the commonwealth absolute sovereigns in their own families, lose afterwards no more of their authority than the law of the commonwealth takes from them.

Private bodies regular but unlawful are those that unite themselves into one representative person without any public authority at all — such as the corporations of beggars, thieves, and gypsies, the better to organise their trade of begging and stealing; and the corporations of men who, by authority from any foreign person, unite themselves in another's dominion, for the easier propagation of doctrines, and for forming a party against the power of the commonwealth.

Irregular systems, being in their nature only leagues, or sometimes mere gatherings of people without union to any particular design, not held together by obligation of one to another but proceeding only from a similarity of wills and inclinations, become lawful or unlawful according to the lawfulness or unlawfulness of each particular man's design in them; and his design is to be understood from the occasion.

Leagues among subjects (since leagues are commonly made for mutual defence) are, in a commonwealth (which is itself nothing more than a league of all the subjects together), for the most part unnecessary, and smack of unlawful design; and are for that reason unlawful, and commonly go under the name of factions, or conspiracies. For a league, being a connection of men by covenant, if there is no power given to any one man or assembly (as in the condition of mere nature) to compel performance, is valid only so long as no just cause of distrust arises. So leagues between commonwealths, over which no human power is established to keep them all in awe, are not only lawful but also profitable for as long as they last. But leagues among the subjects of one and the same commonwealth, where everyone may obtain his right by means of the sovereign power, are unnecessary for the maintaining of peace and justice — and (if the design of them is evil, or unknown to the commonwealth) unlawful. For all united strength among private men is, if for an evil intent, unjust; if for intent unknown, dangerous to the public, and unjustly concealed.

If the sovereign power is in a great assembly, and a number of men, who are part of that assembly, consult apart without authority, to contrive the guidance of the rest, this is a faction, or unlawful conspiracy — being a fraudulent leading of the assembly for their own particular interest. But if a man whose private interest is to be debated and judged in the assembly makes as many friends as he can, in him it is no injustice; in this case he is no part of the assembly. And though he hire such friends with money (unless there is an express law against it), it is still not injustice. For sometimes (such are men's manners) justice cannot be had without money; and every man may think his own cause just until it is heard and judged.

In all commonwealths, if a private man keeps more servants than the government of his estate, and the lawful employment he has for them, requires, it is faction, and unlawful. Having the protection of the commonwealth, he has no need of the defence of private force. And whereas in nations not thoroughly civilised, several great families have lived in continual hostility, and have invaded one another by private force, it is plain enough that they have acted unjustly — or else that they had no commonwealth.

And as factions for kindred, so also factions for the government of religion — as of Papists, Protestants, and so on — or for the form of the state — as Patricians and Plebeians in old time at Rome, and Aristocraticals and Democraticals in old time in Greece — are unjust, as being contrary to the peace and safety of the people, and a taking of the sword out of the hand of the sovereign.

A gathering of people is an irregular system, whose lawfulness or unlawfulness depends on the occasion, and on the number of those assembled. If the occasion is lawful and clear, the gathering is lawful, as in the usual meeting of men at church, or at a public show, in the usual numbers. For if the numbers are extraordinarily great, the occasion is not evident; and consequently he who cannot give a particular and good account of his being among them is to be judged conscious of an unlawful and tumultuous design. It may be lawful for a thousand men to join in a petition to be delivered to a judge or magistrate; yet if a thousand men come to present it, it is a tumultuous assembly, because there need only be one or two for that purpose. But in such cases as these, it is not a fixed number that makes the assembly unlawful, but a number such that the officers on the spot are not able to suppress it and bring it to justice.

When an unusual number of men gather against a man whom they accuse, the assembly is an unlawful tumult, because they could deliver their accusation to the magistrate by a few, or by one man. Such was the case of St Paul at Ephesus, where Demetrius and a great number of other men brought two of Paul's companions before the magistrate, saying with one voice, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians' — which was their way of demanding justice against them for teaching the people doctrine contrary to their religion and to their trade. The occasion here, considering the laws of that people, was just; and yet their assembly was judged unlawful, and the magistrate rebuked them for it in these words (Acts 19:40): 'If Demetrius and the other workmen can accuse any man of anything, there are pleas, and deputies; let them accuse one another. And if you have any other matter to demand, your case may be judged in a lawfully called assembly. For we are in danger of being accused for this day's sedition, because there is no cause by which any man can give any reason for this concourse of people.' There he calls an assembly of which men can give no just account a sedition, and one for which they could not answer. And this is all I shall say about systems and assemblies of people, which (as I said) may be compared to the similar parts of a man's body: those that are lawful, to the muscles; those that are unlawful, to wens, boils, and abscesses, bred by the unnatural inflowing of evil humours.
